newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul central bank moves to block currency's fall.
newsitem.headline: Seoul central bank moves to block currency's fall.

text.p: South Korea's central bank on Tuesday sent a stern signal to currency speculators as the local currency slipped to an all-time low in early trading, dealers said on Tuesday.
In what has become a recent pattern, the central bank intervened in the interbank market in morning trading shortly after the won hit a record low of 901.00 at 0130 GMT, they said.
The bank, following its usual practice, declined to confirm the action, and the won soon rebounded to 899.70.
Aiding the rebound, an assistant governor of the central bank said he believed the dollar had peaked against the won under the current demand and supply.
"Considering the prospects for short- and long-term demand and the supply of dollars, the dollar seems to have peaked versus the won," assistant governor Lee Kang-nam said.
"There are no reasons for the dollar to strengthen further today," he said.
The dollar gained 3.8 won on Monday on import settlements and dollar short-covering combined with the depreciation of other Asian currencies against the dollar.
The depreciation continued on Tuesday on aggressive buying from merchant banks to cover dollar shortages and corporate import settlements.
Lee forecast the dollar would gradually decline against the won from a mid- and long-term point of view.

He said South Korea's overall balance of payments would post a surplus later this year, aided by a reduction in the trade deficit and an inflow of foreign funds following an anticipated expansion of the foreign stock ownership ceiling.
South Korea has said it would raise the foreign shareholding limit in the second half this year from the current 23 percent.
"Since the central bank sees the current dollar level as the peak, the 900 mark would be guarded," one foreign trader said.
Analysts and dealers blamed a recent string of corporate troubles which led to difficulties in overseas borrowing of foreign currencies and rising exchange rate vulnerability.
"Fears that the Korean won could fall under speculators' attack have prompted domestic firms to sell won and buy dollars," said Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Investment Securities.

Lee In-hyung, of LG Economic Research Institute, said: "Financial institutions and corporations are competitively securing dollars on expectations of further financial troubles at local companies and banks."
A corporate crisis which started with the collapse of Hanbo Steel Co in January has pushed down international credit ratings of local debt-laden financial institutions.
